Let’s dive into Chapter 3—Turning Insight Into Action: Diagnosing and Targeting Crucial Moments.
Now that you’ve got a clear map of the six sources of influence, it’s time to zero in on those specific moments when real change either happens… or it falls apart. These are what we call the “crucial moments.” Think of them as the times, places, or situations when old habits are most likely to sneak back in.
Picture someone trying to cut back on spending. Their crucial moments might be as simple as strolling past a favorite store, feeling stressed out after a tough day, or even just browsing online late at night. In each of those situations, the urge to spend is at its peak—and the risk of falling back into old patterns? That’s when it’s highest.
Spotting these moments is like finding the weak links in a chain. If you can focus your attention on those points, you can design strategies that actually prevent relapses and make new behaviors stick.
Here’s a practical way to tackle this:
First, spot the crucial moments. Look for the times, places, or even emotional states that always seem to trigger the unwanted behavior.
Second, analyze what’s going on beneath the surface. Use that six sources framework to figure out why these moments are so tough.
And third, design small, practical changes—targeted strategies that really address those key influences in each moment.
Want an example? Let’s say someone’s trying to eat healthier. They might notice that late-night snacking is a problem, especially when they’re bored or lonely. Personal motivation is low—they’re just looking for comfort. And snacks are easy to grab, so the structural ability is high.
A smart strategy here might be to remove tempting foods from the house—changing the environment. Or maybe find a new evening routine, like calling a friend or reading a good book. That way, you’re boosting both personal motivation and social support.
Here’s another scenario: someone wants to be more productive at work, but they always get distracted after lunch. That post-lunch slump? It’s a classic crucial moment. By digging in, you realize it’s about personal ability—managing energy—and also structural ability, like how their workspace is set up. So, a solution could be taking a short walk to recharge or rearranging the workspace to cut down on distractions.
The real magic of this approach is its specificity. Instead of just saying, “I’ll try harder,” you create concrete actions that fit the moments that matter most. And over time, these small tweaks add up, making new habits feel more natural and sustainable.
But here’s something to pay attention to—crucial moments aren’t always obvious. Sometimes, they’re hidden in your daily routines or triggered by little things you barely notice. That’s where a simple journal or log can make a huge difference, helping you spot patterns you might otherwise miss.
So, here’s the key takeaway: lasting change comes from identifying those moments when old habits are most likely to creep back in—and then designing targeted, practical strategies to handle what’s really driving them. When you do that, you turn change from a vague hope into a clear, step-by-step process.
